entities.name: Berlin Zoological Garden
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Established in 1844, the Berlin Zoological Garden is recognized as the oldest and most renowned zoo in Germany, situated within the expansive Tiergarten in Berlin. Spanning 35 hectares, it houses approximately 1,380 species and over 20,200 animals, constituting one of the most extensive collections of biodiversity in the world. Its establishment marked a significant shift in the way humans interacted with and understood the natural world, promoting conservation and education about wildlife. Key figures in its development included the Prussian King Friedrich Wilhelm IV, who envisioned the zoo as a space for public enjoyment and scientific study, reflecting the era's burgeoning interest in natural history.

The zoo opened its gates to the public in the context of a rapidly industrializing Germany, a time when zoos began to transition from mere menageries to centers of education and conservation. It pioneered the concept of the 'modern zoo', emphasizing naturalistic enclosures that mimic animals' native habitats rather than confining them to barren cages. Throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the institution became a vital site for zoological research and public engagement, contributing significantly to species conservation efforts, including breeding programs for endangered species.

The legacy of the Berlin Zoological Garden extends far beyond its walls; it influenced the establishment of numerous other zoological institutions worldwide, fostering a global awareness of animal conservation. The zoo's innovative approaches to animal husbandry and education have been adopted internationally, shaping contemporary practices in zoology and wildlife preservation. In 1931, it became the first zoo in the world to feature a successful breeding program for the giant panda, an achievement that resonated globally and underscored the zoo's role in international wildlife conservation efforts.
